records.title: Show HN: Coral – Open-source gateway where agents write their own tools
records.author: jcs
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm James, one of the co-founders of Coral.

Coral is an open-source, self-hosted gateway that sits between your agents and the systems they work on. Agents call tools by writing short TypeScript programs that they can save as custom tools to reuse.

You can publish custom tools for groups of agents, so your team’s library of tools adapts to your unique systems, data and use cases. Custom tools help agent performance and give more precise units of permission control.

Here’s a short demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p0PKOlHLyVI

We started on this while building an AI SRE. To investigate an incident, the agent had to connect the dots across an ocean of telemetry data and undocumented relationships across internal and external systems. It took broad permissions, a lot of tokens and it would start from scratch the next time.

We built Coral so that the agent remembers the route. Once a task succeeds, the agent writes the steps that worked into a program and saves it as a custom tool. Next time, the agent finds that custom tool in the same search as standard provider tools (e.g. Datadog, Slack), and reuses it. It started with SRE, but we (and our early users) now use Coral for agent work across the org.

For our tasks across GitHub, Linear and Slack with Opus 5.5, custom tools help agents work 29% faster, at 31% lower cost (tasks here: https://withcoral.com/docs/examples/custom-tools).

Coral builds on code mode, adding custom tools, policy controls and managed identities. Each program runs in a V8 isolate with no network access or credentials. Coral checks every tool call against workspace policy before attaching credentials and forwarding it to the provider. You can configure each provider to use the caller’s own account, so teammates can share tools without sharing API tokens. (e.g. https://withcoral.com/blog/slackbot-works-better-with-coral)

Coral is written in Rust, and you can run it as a desktop app or as a shared server. The core is Apache 2.0 and has no limits on users, agents or volume. Everything I've described here is in the OSS edition. SAML, SCIM, and org-wide governance features will be available soon under an enterprise licence.

We'd love for you to try it and share your feedback. You can download it here https://withcoral.com/download.

I'll be in the comments here and on Slack: https://withcoral.com/slack

records.author: itsmeyaw
records.storyText:
Hi everyone!

Installing skills globally in ~/.agents or ~/.claude consumes too much context, yet manually installing specific skills for every project is tedious. Wouldn't it be better to group skills for programming, backend architecture, or graphic design into collections, and install them with a single command only when needed?

To solve this, I built Skillset. It acts as a wrapper around the Vercel Skill CLI that batch-installs sets of skills from multiple sources using a single JSON file, essentially npm for skills!

While similar tools exist, most are written from scratch, which makes me concerned about their compatibility. Because Vercel’s Skill CLI is already the de facto standard (imo!), Skillset uses it directly as an underlying library. So it guarantees seamless compatibility across teams, regardless of whether they use Skillset or the standard Vercel CLI.

records.title: Show HN: Pizza – An event-driven AI agent, no while true
records.author: tomsun28
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I made Pizza, an open-source, event-driven AI agent. No `while true`.

Each turn is a state machine. Conversations and tool calls go into an immutable SQLite log. The UI, model context, and session tree are built from that log.

The model gets one tool: a CLI. Reading files, editing code, and running commands all go through it.

You can keep a conversation going without manually starting new sessions. Pizza compacts context as needed, and you can branch from any earlier message.

Agents in separate workspaces talk through `tell`, each doing the work in its own project. An SSH host can be a workspace too: Pizza deploys itself there and runs remotely.

Desktop and terminal interfaces are included. Bring your own model.

https://github.com/pizza-agent/pizza

records.title: Show HN: Deslop skill based on corpus-linguistics and psycholinguistics research
records.author: dannypovolotski
records.storyText:
I vibed this deslop skill because I was getting increasingly annoyed that deslop skills for prose relied either on fitting prose into an overly restrictive format (simple-english and iso-24495) or telling AI to rewrite something without providing any tools in the skill to measure the outcome (which more often than not resulted in one slop being replaced with another).

This skill is based on published measurements of how LLM text differs from human text: Reinhart et al.’s comparison of Biber’s grammatical features in human and model writing, Terčon & Dobrovoljc’s survey of 44 studies, Clark, Martin & Mahowald’s work on why AI text is hard to read, and Graphite’s “AI Tells” study, whose released data includes tell lists for nine current models. It’s benchmarked against three corpora in which humans and models answered the same prompts: 9,984 web-article topics from Graphite, 24,322 questions from HC3 and 3,027 advice prompts from ELEPHANT.

It also ships with a scanner that runs before and after each revision. It shows which problems the revision fixed or newly caused, and it catches dropped facts and any tells from the reviser’s own model family.

records.title: Show HN: Bad Apple but it's Strava [video]
records.author: kevinlinxc
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

Here to show off a project that took 18 months, 7KLOC, and more importantly, 194 kilometres of walking! In a nutshell, I wanted to make the famous silhouette animation “Bad Apple” with Strava, which is an exercise tracking app that visualizes where you walk/run on a map. To use the earth as my canvas, I had to do a lot of coding in the prep work to plan where I would walk for each frame of the animation. As I explain in the video, my problem solving/coding steps were something like this:

- split video into frames, determine a good framerate

- detect contours with OpenCV for each frame. Since frames are very diverse, I had to start with some heuristics for choosing contours and ultimately make a GUI to manually curate all 438 of them (e.g. some frames had many small contours while others had a few important ones, and the video is constantly inverting colours). Output of this work was an intermediate json list of x,y coordinates representing the path along contours

- convert these cartesian coordinates into the Universal Transverse Mercator coordinate system, which represents the earth in a cartesian system (as opposed to GPS which doesn’t lend to adding relative distances in degrees very well)

- convert UTM to GPS using a package, then to the GPX file format which is universally accepted

- Import GPX files into an app that shows where I am and where I need to walk (I used Gaia GPS). Then I turned on Strava in the background and walked for ~18 months until this was done.

I also had to make a bunch of custom software to visualize these walks and make montages of them, like a script to pull polylines from the Strava API, a custom polyline renderer, a script to censor my strava activities a bit, and much more. I’m so proud of this work, it feels like it stands out in a sea of code-only bad apple projects that have become easier to automate with AI, and I hope it can go down as one of the greats in the bad apple colossus of work!

Video: https://youtu.be/HxdQawDIlnU GitHub: https://github.com/kevinlinxc/badapple-strava

Happy to answer any questions!

records.title: Show HN: profiler-md converts performance profiles to Markdown
records.author: tomeraberbach
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

profiler-md is a CLI and JS library that converts performance profiles to Markdown across 17 formats (e.g. pprof), 29 profilers (e.g. py-spy), 22 languages (e.g. Rust), and 4 profile types (call stack profiles, call graphs, heap snapshots, and traces).

Earlier this year I tried using AI agents for performance optimization. They weren't very effective because they frequently:

- Speculated about why something was slow from just reading the code

- Made changes, measured the wall time before vs after, and struggled to distinguish real improvements from noise

- Analyzed raw profiles using one-off scripts, which were often subtly incorrect

The issue was that the agents couldn't read a flamegraph like I could. In a flamegraph, I could see what was slow, and when I made changes, I could see whether the targeted work was eliminated. The agents needed a feedback loop like that.

So I wrote a small converter from Node CPU profiles to Markdown. The agents were much more effective when using it, and I realized I also liked reading the Markdown myself!

I felt this had potential, and I use many different programming languages at work, so I decided to build profiler-md. I also wrote an agent skill [1], which I've successfully used to optimize profiler-md itself and its pprof-format dependency (a 78x speedup on a large pprof file [2] and a 3.3x speedup more broadly [3]).

I got to solve some fun problems for this project:

- Making it so that adding a new format, profiler, or profile type is as simple as implementing an interface and adding to a registry. I also have project skills for this!

- Resolving weirdly differing profiler semantics (e.g. around what line numbers mean [4] [5] [6] [7]) by setting up the right interface boundaries.

- Matching functions across profiles for the Markdown diff output. A profile doesn't contain the full code, so this required some heuristics. I evaluated the algorithm by measuring recall (99.9%) and precision (99.7%) on diffs from real version upgrades.

- Designing a call tree renderer that maximizes metrics such as how many of the hottest functions it shows and how much of the profile's self value it covers [8].

I'd love to hear what you think. Try it out and let me know if you have any feedback or questions!

Full disclosure: I work at Anthropic, but this personal project is unrelated to my employer.

[1] https://github.com/TomerAberbach/profiler-md/#skill

[2] https://github.com/DataDog/pprof-format/pull/77

[3] https://github.com/DataDog/pprof-format/pull/107

[4] https://github.com/rbspy/rbspy/issues/409

[5] https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/29240

[6] https://github.com/google/pprof-nodejs/issues/361

[7] https://github.com/NixOS/nix/blob/16fa212a96192479593620e9b9...

[8] https://github.com/TomerAberbach/profiler-md/blob/a1ee95e4b5...

records.title: Show HN: Prettywhale.ai – Generate data pipelines from data samples
records.author: kbiessy
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I’m Kevin, I run product at PrettyWhale.ai, a small team based in France.

We've spent the last few months building a VS Code extension that writes the tedious part of ingestion code from a data sample.

How it works: You give it a CSV or JSON sample. It profiles the fields, you pick the ones to keep, then it suggests transformations you can accept, edit or drop. At the end you get a complete Python project in your workspace that includes all the necessary quality controls: - Pipeline & transformation code - Unit tests - Config files - Documentation

A design choice we care about: the generation of pipeline is driven by a deterministic workflow rather than an endless chat window (no prompting required). We truly believe that the future of integrating AI into tools will involve a redesign of our user interfaces to get the most out of it.

What it doesn’t do yet: it works from a file (CSV or JSON) you already have. It doesn’t connect to databases or API. These features are scheduled for release by the end of the year.

To try it, there’s a VS Code extension: https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=prettywh... You need an account but free with no credit card.

The model runs on our servers, and the samples are not used to train the models.

records.title: Show HN: Strata Architecture
records.author: yrashk
records.storyText:
I've long thought about how we're influenced by CPU architectures, and importantly, their ISAs.

In a discussion at a meetup, I brought up a topic that interested me for a while: how would an ISA that exposes memory and cache interactions in a more explicit way (because if you think about it, memory is very much I/O), as opposed to being smart and predictive on its own?

An obscure interest, of course. Nevertheless, I wanted to build a quick prototype after that.

What ended up transpiring was a bit larger. A multicore architecture with tiered stores, capabilities, a JIT'd emulator, Verilog RTL with a simulator, a small microkernel OS, UI, JIT Forth, an assembler in its own assembly, a bootstrapping C99 compiler, a few games, a visual debugger, and a few other things.

(This also shows just how far a directed LLM process can go in little time)

records.title: Show HN: OpenButterfly – Tracking the environmental impact of the AI ecosystem
records.author: ravipatib
records.storyText:
I built OpenButterfly to help people understand the environmental impact of the AI ecosystem.

Openbutterfly tracks major AI companies (AI labs, cloud providers, chip makers and data center operators) and maps data center sites with their local grid carbon and water stress. Every disclosed figure links to the report page it came from. Missing figures show as "not disclosed", and estimates are clearly labeled.

A few things surprised me. Eight of the 35 companies publish no energy, emissions or water figures at all, and seven of those eight are AI developers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI and DeepSeek. No company publishes how much electricity its AI workloads use. And because of renewable energy certificates, companies typically report only about a fifth of the emissions from the grid power they actually used.

Openbutterfly website itself is maintained by local LLMs (Gemma 4 31B, Qwen 3.8 27B), so its own AI environment footprint stays small. Automated pipelines running local LLMs fetch, extract company figures, and regularly they pick relevant stories from publisher news feeds and write a summary of each.

records.title: Show HN: Nobody blocks a keyboard – Rooted Android as a physical USB Deck
records.author: mr-anjaneyam
records.storyText:
Hey HN, I built Emittr because, i frequently deal with air-gapped or locked-down systems where USB storage is disabled and third party software cannot be installed. Nobody blocks a physical keyboard, so i used the Linux Kernel's USB gadget subsystem (ConfigFS at /dev/hidg0) to turn a rooted android phone to a real USB HID Keyboard and mouse. 1. No installation on target device. It talks to motherboard USB controller, so it works in every locked down OS as well, BIOS, GRUB, etc. 2. Out of band bridge : we don't store passwords or authenticators on rooted phone. Emittr exposes a web UI on LAN, so we can send keystrokes from our main phones. 3. Types long scripts (chatgpt debuggings), SSH keys or passwords at ~1000 WPM without touching the host's clipboard. 4. OS can see this only as a genuine HID keyboard/mouse. Zero host footprint as no drivers, software or background scripts on target machine. 5. Uses USB-IF 0x0238 via on-screen joysticks instead of synthetic Shift + Scroll hacks.

Feel free to check the work and try if you have a rooted android handy. GitHub: https://github.com/mr-anjaneyam/Emittr Webpage: https://emittr.srianjaneyam.me/

I'm planning to record and add few demos in various scenarios (Windows, macOS, android, linux, bios) and devices (Phone, PC, TV, STB, Kiosk).

Happy to answer any questions and would love to hear your suggestions, feature ideas or edge cases.

records.title: Show HN: Hosts Tray – hosts file switcher with built-in HTTPS proxy
records.author: maxmart
records.storyText:
Hi, I'm Max. I've used many hosts file switchers over the years to do local development with real hostnames/domains, combined with HTTPS reverse-proxies.

I made HostsTray to combine both into one tool.

Through a tray icon (Windows) or menu bar (macOS) you can toggle groups of hosts file entries, and toggle the HTTPS proxy.

The HTTPS proxy first installs a local CA cert into your keychain/certificate store, and then uses it to create certificates for each domain that passes through the proxy.

You can configure the proxy to route different paths to different ports locally. Websockets are also supported.

A common problem when editing hosts file is to make Chrome/other browser actually update the DNS cache. I found this is due to Chrome holding a pool of open connections in the background. HostsTray solves this by dropping the open connections to addresses that changed, forcing Chrome to reconnect and re-lookup the hostnames. It is VERY satisfying to toggle a hosts group and see Chrome obey immediately.

Switching can be password-free using an optional helper that runs as admin. The helper only does switching/toggling of groups you already have.

HostsTray also exposes a local API to toggle hosts groups and the proxy. The API also serves a skill suitable for coding agents. So you can let Claude Code toggle for you. It can also add new hostnames to HostsTray, but that requires user verification from you.

The whole thing is a ~10 MB binary written in Go, open-source for Windows and macOS.

Hope this can be useful Feedback is very welcome.

Maintaining agentic skills alway felt like a chore due to how hard it was to test them.

Writing evals is just too complex to do for every small skill, So I wrote Skillroll - an eval framework that can test any skill using only an eval.md

How? instead of setting up an intricate eval environment, you write a short world description, run a Dungeon Master agent that simulates that world, and route all tool calls to that agent.

each eval.md is a test case with a "world description", "agent prompt and "judgement criteria" for an llm judge to consider when rating pass/fail.

I found openai's Luna to be a very nice value-for-money option for running the dungeon master, with cost per eval of around $0.003, and support for pretty complex world scenarios.

I hope it might help you reduce the friction in writing evals for your own skills

records.title: Show HN: Daventry.io – browser game engine inspired by Sierra, ZZT, and D&D
records.author: rdh18
records.storyText:
This started out as a casual side project, tinkering with AI to play some of my favorite old adventure games like King's Quest and Space Quest in the browser. Now it's a self-running, self-maintaining, self-iterating side project capable of importing, playing (single player or multiplayer), or modding those games (manually or with AI), or creating completely new games from scratch. It sort of invented a couple of its own "languages" along the way? It calls one of them the "machine form" which is in the ballpark of LLVM IR and ghidra p-code, and the other one is a TypeScript subset, meant to be a more human-readable layer on top of the machine form. Honestly I'm still trying to catch up a bit on what it's done and continuing to do.

I linked to the "Making Of" page of the app because I think my process and "collaboration" with Claude might actually be even more interesting than the project itself.

As a software engineer, I've been grappling with how to use or not use AI in this new world we're living in. Here's my most optimistic attitude after working on this project:

- Coding before AI was more like building with legos, one piece at a time.

- Coding with AI is more like sculpting, where you already start with material, and you shape and shave and chip off what you don't like until you get something closer to what you want.

For this project, I provided (and sometimes continue to tweak) the main goal and vision. At the beginning I still kicked off each Claude session myself and was actively prompting each step. At some point though, enough documentation had been made that my sessions started becoming one prompt of "what's next" and then a second prompt of "ok, go". So now I have an "ops coordinator" Claude session that runs routinely and spins up additional Claude sessions to keep working on the project...without me. They do things like work through the queue of already-planned work, brainstorm new items to work on, test existing work, do research into related projects or applications, have meetings with each other, and propose new directions or breaking changes to me. If there's something that requires me, I get notified. There are also several Claude html artifacts that function as a a sort of dashboard that I can pull up to see what's been done recently, what's coming up next, and what questions or action items there are for me.

Even though that sounds very hands-off, I find that I'm actually still pretty involved, because I like to redirect and nudge what the agents are working on pretty frequently. And that process does still feel pretty creative and engaging. Hence my "sculpting" attitude.

But, there are other possible metaphors for coding with AI that also come to mind...

- IKEA

- Frankenstein

So at this point, I guess it's still an open question: is what I'm making more of a sculpted work of art, or more like Frankenstein's monster?

records.title: Show HN: Tyrus – TypeScript Syntax. Rust Semantics. Programming Language
records.author: titenq
records.storyText:
Four months ago, I got curious about building my own programming language.

All I wanted was for it to be written in Rust and compiled to native code. My initial goal was simply to print "Hello World" in the terminal. I pulled it off, and from there, I kept adding more features.

I knew absolutely nothing about compilers when I started. Along the way, I discovered a whole new world of concepts: parsing, semantic analysis, AST, ASan, LSan, UB, LLVM, IR, drop glue, double free, LSP, and so on.

Today, I feel like I know maybe 5% of it. Now it's time to fix all the bugs that will inevitably show up.

So I created Tyrus: TypeScript syntax. Rust semantics.

What is already implemented:

- Lexer, parser, and AST - Type checker with inference and generics - Borrow checker with NLL - LLVM codegen - REPL with JIT - Async functions, async/await, and task management - Arrays, tuples, Map, Set, and collection methods - Option/Result, comptime, defer/errdefer, exhaustive pattern matching, and pipe operator - Validator Decorations - Automated tests and a CLI to create, check, build, run, and watch projects - LSP for VS Code, Neovim, Zed, Kate, and IntelliJ/WebStorm - WASM playground - Native modules: fs, os, net, http, process, temporal, crypto, algorithm, archive, compress, db, encoding, stream, task, and others

https://tyruslang.org

What feature would you implement if you were building your own programming language?

records.title: Show HN: Jevmem – Auto Tracked Project Rules for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor
records.author: avinashjetwani
records.storyText:
hi HN, I'm AJ.

Have been using Claude Code every day, and I was done re-typing the same project rules in every new chat. So I built this.

We try to follow some rules in our coding projects. For eg: "we use pnpm, not npm". The problem is, i tell claude about this rule in one chat, when i start another chat, i have to retype it. Also, when my team opens the same repo using another ai tool lets say cursor, they dont see the rule in their chat. Not cool.

So I built jevmem. It saves your project's rules in a file in your repo. and before Claude Code runs a command, it checks the command against those rules.

How it works:

1) You chat with Claude Code like normal.

2) jevmem saves your rules, decisions and everything that failed, one line each, in a file called JEVMEM.md in your repo.

3) You commit JEVMEM.md like any other file.

4) Claude Code, Cursor and Codex can all read it. now, your team also gets it when they pull.

for example: on Mon you tell Claude "we use pnpm, not npm". On Tuesday your teammate pulls and opens the repo in Cursor. They can see the pnpm rule.

oh and guard is my favourite part. So before Claude Code runs a command or edits a file, jevmem checks it against your rules. If it may break one of your rules, Claude Code stops and asks you first.

Eg: your rule is "don't hand-edit db/migrations/, those files are generated". 3weeks later, in a new session if claude tries to edit a migration, Claude Code stops and shows:

jevmem: this may break a saved rule: "Don't hand-edit db/migrations/: those files are generated." (JEVMEM.md)

You can also retrieve failed attempt. Like if you tried caching API responses in memory, and it broke the build, claude will remember that and some time later when you do the same thing, Claude tells you "Already tried: ..." with the reason.

Numbers from our tests:

-> Claude broke a project rule and left it in the code: 0 of 15 sessions with jevmem, 9 of 15 without it. We checked each one by hand.

-> Claude followed decisions made earlier in the project: 66 of 72 sessions with jevmem, 28 of 72 without.

Tbh, a CLAUDE.md file that you keep updating yourself did about as well here (67 of 72). The difference is that jevmem updates the file for you, likewise for cursor and codex.

jevmem also works alongside Claude Code's own auto memory. It doesn't replace it.

The catches:

- The guard works in Claude Code only. - You need a paid TypeSafe API key. jevmem's requests are billed to that key. - Your message text is sent to TypeSafe to be scored. Common secrets are removed first. - Nothing stored remotely. You turn it on per project. - We ran the tests on our own test projects.

(MIT license) Full results: https://avinash-jetwani.github.io/jevmem/results/

Install:

1. In claude: Plugins > Discover > jevmem > Add

2. npm install -g jevmem

3. In your project folder: jevmem setup

Repo: https://github.com/Avinash-jetwani/jevmem

I'd like to hear about your genuine feedback and how we could make it better!

records.title: Show HN: Claktor – a refactoring CLI for coding agents
records.author: mszbednarski
records.storyText:
I've been working on Claktor ever since I got frustrated with some 'code smells' AI Agents have been producing while writing Rust. Claktor is a refactoring tool that leverages custom AST parsing and processing to produce ranked 'leads' on what in the codebase should be looked into to reduce logic duplication. When I started out, it was mostly an opinionated 'how code should be written' detector, after attempting to formalize something objectively useful out of it I've arrived to this.

How is it scored? When exploring how to try to roughly judge how much logic there is in a program, the first approach is LOC. However that is just a proxy as lines can have lots of meat and can be gamed. What we arrived to are 'normalized tokens' which is a parsing of a normalized program by an LLM tokenizer. This neatly fits into then cost of reading the modified file by AI Agents. The more normalized tokens we reduce while preserving behaviour, the more deduplicated to codebase is and cheaper it is to read, extend, test and maintain by AI Agents. (the normalization is subject to some guards like: removing types does not reduce tokens)

Is this developed to the extent that it can be? By all means no! It already is very effective however as it greedily ranks everything through the codebase so AI Agents can remove around 3 to 10 times more for the same cost depending on the repo.

Please try it out and let me know how it goes! Currently works with TS,JS,Rust and Python

records.title: Show HN: Simplex – Self-hosting AArch64 ELF compiler built on a GrapheneOS phone
records.author: mrelf
records.storyText: Simplex is a compiler that strikes directly at the architectural heresy of modern computing, spitting out pure, self-contained ELF64 AArch64 Linux executables directly on the metal. A recursive descent parser feeds a code generator that encodes A64 machine instructions by hand into three segments, text, rodata and BSS. The language has one type, with raw pointers and byte intrinsics. And it is self-hosting: the compiler compiles its own source, and the next two generations come out bit-identical. To fully appreciate the tragedy of modern computing, I coded and bootstrapped the entire system on a smartphone running GrapheneOS, inside Termux, wrapped in PRoot, running my custom Void Linux musl rootfs.

records.title: Show HN: Apertrue Witness – proof of camera and identity for video calls
records.author: stablepixel
records.storyText:
Hi HN. This all started when I was targeted by one of those fake video call schemes we hear so much about lately. I was invited into a video call with someone posing as a person I’d met at a conference, and I was close to being fooled before their “audio problems” became increasingly suspicious. When Tavus announced its Griffin-Lite model last month, they claimed 48% of callers mistook it for a human. I think to avoid future scenarios like my own, it’s clear we need irrefutable proof of who’s on the other side of your call and not simply a judgement call.

So I’ve been working these last few months on a solution that proves the person on the other side of a call is using a genuine camera and is who they say they are, without sacrificing privacy and avoiding the pitfalls of using detection.

The result is Apertrue Witness. You can find details on how it works in the first comment, on the landing page, and full technical detail here (https://witness.apertrue.photo/how).

records.title: Show HN: 1MB Tenstorrent driver with ptx like kernels
records.author: zk4x
records.storyText: The world of AI used to have people training models for solving substantial issues - like beat world's best go players or solving protein folding. Now that the AI got good, perhaps we forgot a bit how to do it. There is still cheap hardware around for tinkerers and people who want to continue good AI legacy. But the hardware may miss software. It is for those people that I started working on zyx long time ago - ML library in hopes of running on any hardware. One example of such hardware is tenstorrent. But the basics must be built first. And so today I'm showing you skamandros. A tiny, self-contained driver and compiler for tenstorrent cards (tested on p100a). PTX like input, mostly abstracted away hardware details (other than tiling), automatic optimizations and operation fusion. Hope you can use this software to write AI models that people can like.

records.title: Show HN: atl, a Rust CLI for Jira, Confluence and Bitbucket with ~15ms overhead
records.author: racetozero
records.storyText:
Hello HN,

I built `atl`, a Rust CLI for Jira, Confluence, Bitbucket, Jira Service Management, Trello and Atlassian Admin. The same commands work on Cloud and Data Center (on-prem).

It's built for both people and AI agents: an --agent mode that outputs JSON and never prompts, a built-in MCP server with 136 tools, and a read-only login so an agent can't change anything. Confluence pages can be edited as Markdown and kept in git.

It has SDK support as well for Python, TypeScript/JS, and WASM.

Any feedback and contributions are welcome!

records.title: Show HN: PongArena – Play Pong and see how tiny neural networks think
records.author: nrjl
records.storyText:
A playground and experiment exploring "how small can a neural network be and still meaningfully play Pong?" You can play against the models directly in your browser, also on mobile, no signup needed. Recommend hitting the fullscreen button for better gameplay.

The discussion https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50341174 sparked my interest and I started experimenting a bit with generating neural network weights. I used Codex to program the weights, developing formulas that generate them and refining them using feedback from simulated matches. I also tried one-shot prompting Astra for the weights directly.

The surprise, I think, is how hard it’s been in my training attempts to outperform the programmed model using the same 163-parameter architecture.

The playground also has some explainers to help interpret the weights, starting from a one-hidden-neuron example with just 13 parameters...

It’s all open source, and there is also a league where community weights can be submitted. It would be interesting to see how others would approach this. Can anyone train, prompt or program weights that outperform the initial ones?

Code: https://github.com/jonaslindblom/pongarena
